opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the cleanest way to see it is to count how much information each update actually carries.

In supervised learning, say next-token prediction, every token gives you a full target. You're telling the model "the right answer was exactly this token, out of fifty thousand or a hundred thousand options." That's on the order of log of the vocabulary size, maybe fifteen-plus bits of signal per token, and you get it at every position in the sequence. So a thousand-token document is thousands of dense, precise corrections.

Now take reinforcement learning with an outcome reward. The model generates a whole trajectory, maybe hundreds or thousands of tokens, and at the end you get a scalar: it worked or it didn't. In the binary case that's at most one bit for the entire episode, and you then have to spread that one bit across every decision that led to it. That's the credit assignment problem. Which of those thousand tokens was the good one? The gradient doesn't really know; it just nudges everything in the trajectory up or down a little.

And here's the part that matters for an *untrained* model: if the policy is random, the probability of ever hitting a reward is basically zero for any interesting task. Producing a correct proof or a working program by sampling uniformly from the vocabulary just never happens. So you don't merely get a weak signal, you get no signal at all, because every rollout scores zero and there's nothing to contrast against. RL fundamentally needs the policy to already land in the neighborhood of success some meaningful fraction of the time.

That's why I think of pretraining and RL as doing really different jobs. Pretraining is the high-bandwidth phase where you pour enormous amounts of information about the world into the weights. It builds a prior where good behaviors are at least occasionally sampled. Then RL acts more like a selection mechanism on top of that prior. It's saying, "of the things you already know how to do, do more of these and fewer of those." It's very good at sharpening and at eliciting capabilities, and it can compose things in new ways, but it's a low-bandwidth channel for injecting genuinely new knowledge.

There's a nice analogy to evolution versus learning within a lifetime. Evolution is a one-bit-per-lifetime signal, roughly "did you reproduce," and it took an absurd amount of compute across billions of organisms to get anywhere. Whereas a kid learning language gets dense feedback constantly. Applying RL to a blank-slate network is kind of like asking evolution to do the job of a schoolteacher.

The interesting research question to me is how much you can densify the RL signal: process rewards, learned value functions, having the model critique its own intermediate steps. Each of those is basically an attempt to recover some of the bits-per-token that supervised learning gives you for free, without needing a human to write down the answer.

r001.rationale: The response says supervised learning provides dense, token-level targets, while an RL outcome gives at most one bit across an entire trajectory. It does not say a correct sampled word gives as much learning as supervised learning.

r002.rationale: It explains that an untrained model’s unsuccessful rollouts provide no signal to contrast against, and that an outcome signal is spread across all decisions in the trajectory.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is in terms of bits of information per episode, per sample. With supervised learning, every token you're predicting gives you a dense gradient. You're told exactly what the right next token was, so you get something like log of vocabulary size bits of signal on every single position. If you have a thousand-token sequence, that's a thousand corrections packed into one example.

With RL, you roll out a whole trajectory, maybe thousands of tokens, and at the end you get a scalar. Did you win or lose, did the unit test pass or fail. That's on the order of one bit per episode. So in terms of raw information throughput, RL is something like a thousand times worse, maybe more. And that's why people were skeptical of RL for so long, right? It seemed hopeless to train from scratch that way. An untrained model is basically emitting noise, and if you're sampling random token sequences and waiting for one of them to accidentally solve a math problem, you'll wait forever. The reward is never nonzero, so there's no gradient, there's nothing to learn from.

But I think the framing of bits per sample is a little misleading, because what matters isn't the bits you receive, it's the bits you actually needed. Supervised learning is dense, but it's also kind of wasteful. You're spending most of your capacity learning to imitate things that don't matter, the stylistic quirks of whoever wrote the data, the exact phrasing, and you're not getting any signal about whether the overall behavior was good. You can perfectly imitate a demonstrator who is wrong.

RL's one bit is a much more precious bit. It's about the thing you actually care about. And crucially, the model gets to pick what it's being graded on, because it generated the trajectory. So that bit is targeted at the model's own current distribution, which is exactly where supervised learning is weakest, this distribution shift problem where you train on the expert's states and then at test time you're in states the expert never visited.

So the way I'd put it is, pretraining buys you a model where the probability of a good trajectory is no longer astronomically small, maybe it's one in a hundred or one in a thousand instead of one in ten to the thousand. And once you're in that regime, the sparse signal from RL is suddenly worth a lot, because now you're sampling, you're occasionally succeeding, and each success tells the model something no amount of imitation could, which is that this particular thing you did, on your own, actually worked. That's the part people underestimate. The signal isn't just smaller, it's a different kind of signal.

r001.rationale: The response says RL success provides a sparse, different kind of signal, but does not say that sampling the correct word teaches as much as supervised learning on that word.

r002.rationale: It says an untrained model’s random samples rarely succeed and that when reward is absent, there is no gradient and nothing to learn, communicating that incorrect samples provide very little signal.

astra-6.text:
I think the key difference is how much information you get from each example. In supervised learning, you’re telling the model, “Given this context, here’s the token you should have predicted.” Even if the model is completely untrained, that’s a useful signal. You’re pointing it toward a particular answer.

With reinforcement learning, the model has to produce something, and then you tell it how good that was. You’re not necessarily telling it what it should have done instead. So if an untrained language model generates gibberish and gets a reward of zero, there are an enormous number of other things it could try, and most of those will also be gibberish. It’s very hard to get traction.

That’s why pretraining makes such a big difference. Once the model can generate plausible answers, reinforcement learning can distinguish between them and reinforce the better ones. It can potentially discover solutions you didn’t have demonstrations for. But you need enough exploration to encounter something worth reinforcing, and starting from a pretrained model makes that dramatically easier.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts supervised token guidance with reinforcement learning’s reward signal, but does not say that sampling the correct word yields as much learning as supervised learning on that word.

r002.rationale: It says an untrained model that generates gibberish and gets zero reward has many alternatives, most also gibberish, making it “very hard to get traction”—communicating that feedback for an incorrect sample provides little learning signal.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key difference is how much information you get from each example. With supervised learning, you’re telling the model, “Here’s the answer you should have produced.” Even if it starts out completely random, it gets a useful gradient toward that answer at every token.

With reinforcement learning, the model produces something and you tell it how good that was. If it’s untrained, almost everything it produces is garbage. So a reward that just says whether it got the answer right gives it very little information about what to change. It has to discover something worth reinforcing through exploration.

That’s why the starting point matters so much. Once the model can already produce plausible solutions, reinforcement learning can help it figure out which of those solutions work. But getting from random behavior to that point with a sparse reward is a much harder problem.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts supervised token-level gradients with sparse RL rewards, but does not state that sampling the correct word teaches as much as supervised learning on that word.

r002.rationale: It says an untrained model usually produces garbage and that a reward indicating whether the answer was right provides very little information about what to change, conveying that an incorrect sampled outcome gives little learning signal.
